content.summary_of_the_paper:
InstaHide was proposed a few years ago as a way of achieving private ML by "encoding/encrypting" input instances before running ML algorithms on them. That scheme got broken eventually. The key idea behind InstaHide was to only use the "augmented data" that were the result of k-way mix-up operations (plus random flipping of the features).

This paper presents a variant of InstaHide scheme, in which the instances are encoded with a slightly different method. In particular, after the k-way mix-up operations, there is a Laplacian noise that is also added to the instances, before they are fed to the learning algorithm. For a privacy guarantee for their DP-IH scheme, they show that it provides better DP (in pure form, with better eps) than the scheme that merely uses the Laplacian noise.

As another (primary) application for their, so-called, DP-InstaHide scheme, they evaluate their encoding mechanism against *poisoning* attacks. These are attacks that manipulate the training set to increase the risk of the model; some variants even know the test instance, in which case are called "targeted". Note that this is a different application than privacy itself, but it is somehow known in previous work that DP guarantees provide resistance against data poisoning.

The paper then does an in-depth empirical analysis of their scheme's resistance against a variety of poisoning attack's.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The strengths:

- proposing a way of achieving DP mechanisms through k-way mix-ups + noise.
- evaluating the robustness of the *specific* proposed method against poisoning attacks.

Weaknesses:

- both ideas of (1) using mix-up + noise to achieve privacy and (2) using private schemes as a way of defending against poisoning, are known in previous work. (1) was previously studied for Gaussian noise in a cited work from ISIT'19, (though the paper makes the case that their bound was hard to compute.)

- the presentation is not super clear. In particular, it is a bit hard to interpret Theorem 2, as it does not put things in the context of what it is being compared with.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper provides codes, so reproducibility is not an issue.

The writing is not very clear. E.g., see the comment about Theorem 2 above. In particular, to compare something with the vanilla Laplacian mechanism, the utilities should be compared to as well; as otherwise it is intuitively clear that \infty-way mixup will give us a mechanism that is fully private. 

The attack sections are also not very easy to grasp. What measures were used for picking these attacks and defenses for comparison?

Some links are broken (search for ?? in the paper). 

What are HTBD and CLBD?
content.summary_of_the_review:
I think the paper has a merit in modifying the InstaHide scheme into something with better foundations.

On the other hand, the paper seems to miss a truly novel aspect to make it at the level of ICLR; as mentioned above, both ideas of "privacy through mix-up" and "defending poisoning by privacy" were known. Having said that, the demonstration of usefulness of these mechanisms for defending poisoning is interesting and so the paper can still appear and be useful in some venues.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies the privacy guarantees of Mixup+Laplachian noise. In addition, the paper studies the effect of data augmentation in defending against poisoning and backdoor attacks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 

- The paper examines privacy guarantees associated with mixup and Laplacian noise.

Weaknesses:
- Much of experimental evaluation is devoted to showing the efficacy of data augmentation to defend against backdoor and poisoning attacks. However, this has already been studied in past work: Strong data augmentation sanitizes poisoning and backdoor attacks without an accuracy tradeoff. Borgnia et al. 2020. The paper can be improved by better identifying its contributions.
- For many results reported in the paper, only attack success rate is shown. It's known that there is a tradeoff between robustness and accuracy. It'll be good to also report the model accuracy after the defense.
- The baselines compared in the paper are out-dated. For instance, for data poisoning, these two papers achieve the state-of-the-art performance: "Friendly Noise against Adversarial Noise: A Powerful Defense against Data Poisoning Attacks," "Not All Poisons are Created Equal: Robust Training against Data Poisoning." For backdoor, there are a fruitful research on detecting backdoor attacks and mitigating their effect. To name a few: "Anti-Backdoor Learning: Training Clean Models on Poisoned Data," etc. It'll be good to update the related work and baselines with more up-to-date works.
- Several references are missing.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper's written clearly. The reviewer has concerns about quality and novelty as detailed above. The method proposed in the paper is simple and should be easily reproduced.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper studies an important problem of defending against poisoning and backdoor attacks. However, the evaluation largely overlaps with past work and limited new insights are provided. Moreover, evaluation metrics in the paper need to be refined.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper studies data augmentations to enhance privacy guarantees against dataset manipulations. 
In particular, they mainly utilize the InstaHide algorithm to privatize data by first applying mixup, and then multiplying the results by random binary masks.  This paper additionally considers the Differential privacy in the InstaHide defense. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The research problem is very important and this paper provides different aspects to provide enhanced privacy guarantee. 
2. This paper is easy to follow and clearly written.  


Weaknesses

There are some concerns regarding this paper.
1. This paper needs to pay more effort to proofread writing. There are many typos and missing information in the paper.

2. The novelty of this paper is limited. The proposed method is poorly described and motivated. 
For instance, it is still unclear why InstaHide (mixup augmentation)+ Differential privacy. 

3. In experiments, this paper mainly focuses on comparisons with Mixup methods, while some advanced DP defense methods can make this paper better in the experiments.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The novelty of this paper is limited. The proposed method is poorly described and motivated.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper provides formal guarantees for a differentially private version of the InstaHide algorithm, a method which attempts to privatize data by averaging and a random binary mask. This paper modifies the algorithm by replacing the random binary mask with an application of the Laplace mechanism. The paper provides a formal analysis for the privacy guarantees of their algorithm as well as empirical evidence to support their claim.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
The paper provides formal guarantees for an algorithm which previously was only supported empirically. The presentation of the paper is reasonably clear and gives detailed context for the problem at hand. The authors provide a number of experiments to support their claim.

Weaknesses:
The paper is missing vital context from the broader DP literature (e.g. privacy amplification via subsampling). The algorithm presented mirrors what are now standard techniques for ensuring data privacy, and has limited novelty. On a more minor note, there are several undefined variables and broken references.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
My primary concern is that the mechanism proposed by the authors is a standard technique in the DP literature (see for example [1]), and the proof seems to miss out on some analysis that could provide even better guarantees. The mechanism proposed is to randomly sample a subset of k images, take the average, and apply the Laplace mechanism. It is well known that taking a random subsample amplifies privacy [2]. Furthermore, taking the average of k images leads to a reduction in sensitivity by 1/k, also leading to stronger privacy guarantees (under a fixed amount of noise). The authors establish this latter fact in their proof but the analysis is much more complicated than necessary. 

[1] Abadi, M., Chu, A., Goodfellow, I.J., McMahan, H.B., Mironov, I., Talwar, K., & Zhang, L. (2016). Deep Learning with Differential Privacy. Proceedings of the 2016 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security.
[2] Balle, B., Barthe, G., & Gaboardi, M. (2018). Privacy Amplification by Subsampling: Tight Analyses via Couplings and Divergences. ArXiv, abs/1807.01647.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper lacks novelty and misses important context from the DP literature. The main result is an existing result from the DP literature with a more complicated analysis.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
